data.headline: Rip Current Statement issued October 19 at 1:40AM EDT until October 22 at 8:00PM EDT by NWS Miami FL
data.description:
* WHAT...Dangerous rip currents expected.

* WHERE...Coastal Palm Beach County, Coastal Broward County and
Coastal Miami Dade County.

* WHEN...From late tonight through Thursday evening.

* IMPACTS...Rip currents can sweep even the best swimmers away
from shore into deeper water.
data.instruction:
Swim near a lifeguard. If caught in a rip current, relax and
float. Don't swim against the current. If able, swim in a
direction following the shoreline. If unable to escape, face the
shore and call or wave for help.

Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Miami FL
115 PM EDT Mon Oct 19 2026

...New SHORT TERM, AVIATION...

.KEY MESSAGES...
Updated at 107 PM EDT Mon Oct 19 2026

 - Stronger wind gusts continue early this week along with
   hazardous marine and beach conditions for the next few days. 
   Elevated seas and near Gale force winds will be observed.

 - Drier conditions early this week with only some isolated weak
   shower activity possible across SE Florida.

&&

.SHORT TERM...
(Rest of today through Tuesday)
Issued at 107 PM EDT Mon Oct 19 2026

It is exceptionally dry out there today with respect to atmospheric 
moisture content across South Florida. Current mesoanalysis shows 
PWATs ranging between 1.1 and 1.3", which are within the 20th and 
30th percentiles for the date according to HREF guidance. Both the 
12Z MFL and regional ACARS soundings show an immense dry layer in 
the mid to upper levels in tandem with a distinguishable moist layer 
in the lower levels roughly between the first 1-3 km of the 
atmosphere. Looking at the bigger picture as to why this abundance 
of dry air is in place, a sharp longwave upper trough has continued 
to dig further south into South Florida, allowing dry air advection 
to occur on the upstream side of it. Latest surface analysis map 
from the Weather Prediction Center (WPC) shows an anomalously strong 
ridge of high pressure reading 1035 mb (which remains near the upper 
echelon of climatology for this time of year) still centered well to 
our north around the vicinity of the Allegheny Mountains in 
Pennsylvania. To our south, we continue to have a stalled frontal 
boundary over the Florida Straits and near the proximity of northern 
Cuba, which is where we precisely find the highest moisture content 
(generalized PWATs of 1.5-2.0") with widely scattered showers and 
isolated thunderstorms inhabiting this maritime region.

Despite our atmospheric column being so dry, we are still expected 
to have isolated showers (coverage of 10-20% as per our PoPs) 
develop across South Florida today as they move briskly to the 
southwest along our prevailing northeasterly surface flow (which 
continues to be caused by the tight pressure gradient between the 
record-strong high to our north and the stalled frontal boundary to 
our south). Given the overall layout of the atmospheric profile 
today, these showers should be fairly short-lived and shallow-
layered as they swipe across our peninsula. This light to perhaps 
occasionally moderate precipitation should be able to penetrate far 
enough inland this afternoon to possibly bring some flimsy rainfall 
to the interior around the Lake Okeechobee region and portions of 
the western half of South Florida. Once we lose the component of 
diurnal heating tonight, isolated showers should stay relatively 
confined to the east coast as they push onshore from the Atlantic. 
Shouldn't be more than just some nuisance rain to mist at times with 
no flood threat to be concerned about. Similar to yesterday, it will 
stay breezy across South Florida with winds gusting out of the 
northeast to around 25-35 mph.

Should be a copy and paste forecast for tomorrow, with a plethora of 
dry air staying in place across South Florida but enough low-level 
moisture to support the development of isolated showers, mainly 
across the east coast with PoPs below 20%. Model guidance shows the 
ridge axis over the Allegheny Mountains shifting a bit to the north 
toward the Canadian border tomorrow, which should allow our winds to 
come down just by a sliver, but to no avail with respect to our 
local impacts. With MSLPs (mean sea-level pressure) expected to 
remain well above average for this time of year around the vicinity 
of the Great Lakes and a regional pressure gradient still existing 
across our region, it is forecast to be another breezy day with NBM 
guidance suggesting northeasterly wind gusts of 20-30 mph across 
much of South Florida.

High temperatures will stay nice and comfortable in the low to mid 
80s across South Florida today (which is right around where we 
should be this time of year) and Tuesday due to the breezier-than-
normal conditions and a drier and less humid air mass having 
filtered down the peninsula behind our stalled front to the south. 
It will take another day or two for those across Southeast Florida 
to feel the modest but pleasant drop in low temperatures; but those 
around the Lake, over the interior, and along the Gulf coast will 
already be waking up to temperatures in the mid to upper 60s Tuesday 
morning while the east coast metros will settle for the mid 70s. 
Hang in there, the slight cooldown is coming!

&&

.LONG TERM...
(Tuesday night through Sunday)
Issued at 122 AM EDT Mon Oct 19 2026

For the middle of end of this week, enhanced jet stream dynamics 
in the western US will enhance the development of a deep trough 
out west, which in return will strengthen the ridge over the 
central US and an upper level trough across the Eastern Seaboard. 
At the same time, guidance is hinting at a return in deeper 
moisture to average or slightly above average levels. With upper- 
level high pressure providing some forcing for ascent along with 
diurnal processes, rain chances will begin to increase again for 
the end of this week and upcoming weekend. Mid-level and upper- 
level flow for this time period will shift to the SW as the region
will sit on the downstream side of the trough pattern, which will
favor the highest rain chances across SE Florida between 30-50%. 
Uncertainty remains in how much rain could be seen, but currently
this setup is not anticipated to result in the type of rainfall 
we saw this past weekend. 

High temperatures for the middle to end of this week and into next 
weekend are expected in the low to mid 80s each day, with overnight 
lows ranging from the low to mid 60s for SW Florida to the upper 60s 
and low 70s for SE Florida.

&&

.AVIATION...
(18Z TAFS)
Issued at 107 PM EDT Mon Oct 19 2026

Generally VFR through the period save for brief bouts of sub-VFR
at terminals directly impacted by fast-moving SHRA. Gusty NE winds
will become more NNE through the period as shower chances diminish
tonight.


&&

.MARINE...
Issued at 122 AM EDT Mon Oct 19 2026

Hazardous conditions will continue early this week as a strong 
pressure gradient is present and a system near the Mid-Atlantic 
continues to produce a large NE swell. Strong winds at 20-30 kts 
with gusts occasionally reaching near Gale force are expected today 
before starting to decrease mid-week. In addition, seas will remain 
10-14 feet in the Atlantic today and 6-8 feet in the Gulf before 
slowly decreasing in the mid-week period. Seas are expected to 
remain at 8-10 feet in the Atlantic through at least Wednesday. 
Small Craft Advisories remain in effect through Wednesday across all 
local waters, including Biscayne Bay and Lake Okeechobee. 

&&

.BEACHES...
Issued at 122 AM EDT Mon Oct 19 2026

A high risk for rip currents continues for all Atlantic coast 
beaches early this week as strong northeasterly winds and swell 
continue. In addition, large breaking waves of 7-9 feet in the Palm 
Beaches surf zone keeps a High Surf Advisory in effect through 
Tuesday, with the Broward beaches added to the advisory on Tuesday.

&&

TWOAT 

Tropical Weather Outlook
NWS National Hurricane Center Miami FL
800 AM EDT Mon Oct 19 2026

For the North Atlantic...Caribbean Sea and the Gulf of America:

Off the East Coast of the United States:
A storm-force non-tropical low pressure area is located along a 
frontal boundary a few hundred miles off the southeast coast of the 
United States. This low is likely to move slowly and erratically 
over the next couple of days. If the low remains over the Gulf 
Stream and becomes detached from the front, it could briefly acquire 
some subtropical cyclone characteristics during the middle to latter 
portions of the week. The system is expected to begin to move 
northeastward away from the the eastern United States later this 
week, and environmental conditions are expected to become 
unfavorable for development by the weekend.  Regardless of the 
status of the system, high winds, coastal flooding, and dangerous 
surf are expected along portions of the U.S. East Coast during the 
next few days. Please consult statements and warnings from local 
National Weather Service offices and the Weather Prediction Center 
for more information, along with High Seas Forecasts and Storm 
Warnings issued by the National Weather Service.
* Formation chance through 48 hours...low...near 0 percent.
* Formation chance through 7 days...medium...40 percent.

&&
High Seas Forecasts issued by the National Weather Service can be 
found under AWIPS header NFDHSFAT1, WMO header FZNT01 KWBC, and 
online at ocean.weather.gov/shtml/NFDHSFAT1.php

$$
Forecaster Pasch
